newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper says bomb nearly hit his plane.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper says bomb nearly hit his plane.

text.p: Colombian President Ernesto Samper said on Thursday that he had survived a possible assassination attempt involving an attack on his presidential jet.

Speaking in a Reuter interview, Samper said the attempt involved a bomb that exploded near the runway of the airport in Colombia's steamy Caribbean port of Barranquilla, minutes before the presidential aircraft was due to land there Wednesday afternoon.
Initial reports said the bomb exploded up to 2.5 miles (4 km) from the airport runway and represented no real threat to Samper's Dutch-made Fokker aircraft.

But Samper said the explosive device, comprised of 44 pounds (20 kg) of dynamite and an undetermined quantity of birdshot, exploded "just a few meters (yards) away from the head of the runway" and had apparently been intended to detonate seconds before the plane passed over it.
"It was supposed to explode just as the plane was approaching the airstrip," he said.

An air force official, hearing Samper's account of what happened, said the president was lucky indeed that the device went off while the plane was still a good distance from the runway. The explosion, and resulting vacuum, could easily have destabilised the aircraft and cause it to crash, the official said.
Birdshot and shrapnel from the bomb could also, conceivably, have blinded the aircraft's pilot or damaged its engines and fuel tanks.
"It's possible," Samper said when asked if he thought someone had tried to assassinate him. "But it's something it's best not to speculate about."
His jet was put in a holding pattern over Barranquilla immedately after the blast but cleared for landing a short while later.

"I don't remember ever having to wait to land somewhere before," he told an aide at the Casa de Narino presidential palace, half jokingly. "I thought it was a problem with the controllers," he added, saying he thought they had suddenly decided to join in a nationwide strike by public sector workers that began Tuesday.
The portly Samper, 46, still carries four of the 11 bullets fired at him by right-wing hitmen at Bogota's international airport in March 1989 as he stood talking to a left-wing political leader.

He spent days in a coma and needed 22 operations to recover from the attack, which gave him the reputation, especially as he fought off repeated calls for his resignation because of drug corruption charges last year, as a thick-skinned politician with an uncanny instinct for survival.
Samper, who was back in Bogota on Thursday, flew to Barranquilla to watch a World Cup soccer qualifying match between Colombia and Argentina. Colombia lost 1-0.
The Colombian leader frequently refers to his country as "the world's most violent" and says he has been the target of dozens of botched assassination attempts since he took office in August 1994.
There was no claim of responsibility for the latest apparent attempt.
